stances.claim: The new ULAS program will require all lawyers to render at least 60 hours of pro bono legal aid every three years -- an 'earth-shaking' reform with broad enforcement scope.

The draft Rules properly broaden creditable pro bono service beyond litigation to all forms of legal application -- recognizing that non-litigation lawyers can serve qualified beneficiaries in their own fields of expertise.

Beneficiaries are carefully defined: (a) indigents (per Revised Rules of Court or by Affidavit of Indigency); (b) marginalized-sector members for public-interest cases; (c) NGOs and nonprofits whose work benefits indigents and marginalized sectors.

The SC's constitutional justification holds: practice of law is 'imbued with public interest,' and membership in the Bar is 'a special privilege burdened with conditions' -- including the duty to make legal services accessible to the public.
Even 'abogados de campanilla' charging up to $1,000 per hour will be reached: 60 hours of pro bono service is worth $60,000 -- illustrating the program's redistributive bite.

notable_anecdotes: The arithmetic punch: 60 hours × $1,000/hour = $60,000 -- equivalent value of pro bono service from top-tier 'abogados de campanilla' (a phrase translating roughly as 'top-billing lawyers').
The benediction-style closing: 'God bless the Supreme Court and the lawyers. May they never tire of aiding the poor.'

Itemized service categories that explicitly include developmental legal assistance, rights awareness, capacity building, and mentorship under the Law Student Practice Rule -- broadening the operational scope.

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court plans to require all Philippine lawyers to render at least 60 hours of pro bono legal aid services to the poor every three years throughout their professional career under its new Unified Legal Aid Services (ULAS) program. A Technical Working Group chaired by Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa, with Justice Rodil V. Zalameda as vice chair, drafted the ULAS Rules, and the Court has launched a four-leg Regional Consultation series keynoted by Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo: Baguio (April 12), Cagayan de Oro (April 18), Makati (May 17), and Iloilo (TBA). The new Rules will replace earlier initiatives that limited creditable legal aid to litigation work; they will credit 'any service involving the application of law' across non-litigation practice areas, allowing lawyers in their respective fields to serve 'qualified beneficiaries': (a) indigents (per Revised Rules of Court or by Affidavit of Indigency), (b) marginalized-sector members with respect to their public-interest cases -- farmer-peasant, artisanal fisherfolk, formal and informal-sector workers, migrant workers, indigenous peoples and cultural communities, women, differently abled persons, senior citizens, victims of calamities and disasters, youth and students, children, and urban poor -- and (c) NGOs and nonprofits whose work benefits (a) and (b). Creditable pro bono services include court and quasi-judicial representation (with mediation and ADR); legal counseling and contract negotiation/drafting; developmental legal assistance (rights awareness, capacity building, training in human rights, documentation, affidavit-making); participation in Accredited Legal Outreach Programs and Missions including mentorship under the Law Student Practice Rule; and other services as the SC may define. 'Public-interest cases' cover civil rights and liberties, women's rights, children and youth services, workers' rights, employment law, public benefits, gender and sexuality issues, environmental law, prisoners' rights, criminal law, and the death penalty. Enforcement starts January 1, 2025 and will be 'earth-shaking' -- reaching even 'abogados de campanilla' who charge up to $1,000 per hour (research and travel included), making 60 pro bono hours worth $60,000 in foregone billings. The Court justifies the rule on the constitutional ground that the practice of law is 'imbued with public interest' and that 'membership in the Bar is a special privilege burdened with conditions' -- including the duty to make legal services readily accessible to the public. CJ closes: 'God bless the Supreme Court and the lawyers. May they never tire of aiding the poor.'
